en: This brief introduction summarizes the thirty-two sections of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which consist of the dialogues between Śākyamuni Buddha and his disciples.

As it was transmitted to China, those among both monastics and laypeople who recite it have become increasingly numerous; yet, many daily recite it with reverence without maintaining right mindfulness.
I have merely sought to record his many deeds; I did not realize that the two characters "Vajra" (Jingang) encompass infinite meanings.
Now, the nature of gold is firm and hard; it cannot be diminished even by smelting and refining. This is used as a metaphor for the nature of man:

eternally present and as if existing before one's eyes, unpolished throughout kalpas. Though it departs, it returns; though it comes, it departs again. Thus it comes and goes, coming and going repeatedly.
When will this be brought to completion? Not knowing how to practice cultivation, one should have no place of abiding; how then can one attain the Right Path, which is neither going nor coming?
Thus the Confucians say: "That which is mandated by Heaven is called nature. All recognize this within it. Furthermore, they say: "The Center is the Right Path of all under heaven.
To know this path of central rectitude is to recognize the firmness and hardness of the nature of gold. I lost my father while still young.
In my youth, I was dull-witted in my studies; only recently have I reached this age. My mother’s resolve was as firm as the *Boat of Cypress* (*Bai Zhou*).

Now that more than forty-six years have passed, she has reached the venerable age of seventy-five. Whenever I think of my aged mother, who maintained such bitter austerity, how can I ever fully repay her kindness? Because our family was poor...

While traveling as a guest to Tianjin, I was fortunate to encounter an enlightened teacher who instructed me that only by maintaining the precepts and fasts with purity can one repay the fundamental debt of gratitude.

At this, I became suddenly awakened and my base resolve was instantly transformed. Having received his instructions, I applied myself most sincerely to the precepts and fasts; he pointed out the ford for me across the sea of delusion, and only then did I clearly realize my true nature.
The vow to repay my mother now has its appointed time. How may one clarify this true nature? It is what is referred to as the two aspects of the *Vajra* [Sūtra].
[The author] Zixun believed its nature to be thus. In the winter of that year, while he was initially staying as a guest in Gusu, the two gentlemen Xia and Lin visited him.

They produced from their sleeves the *Jingang Tieqiangjin Jie* (Exegesis on the Diamond Sutra’s Iron Spikes) and presented it to him. Upon examining it, he found its flavor to be profound and far-reaching;

every sentence remained correct, and every character accorded with the Middle Way. Therefore, he had it re-carved for circulation in the world. All who recite the *Diamond Sutra* must carefully examine its underlying principles before proceeding.
This clarifies the causes for transcending the world; it is truly intended for the purpose of a hand-mirror.
Written on the first day of the first month of the Wuzi year of the Shunzhi era, by the layman Yizhi of Keshan, Gong Taisheng, father of Linsheng, with hands washed in reverence.
I have now seen, heard, received,
and upheld this unsurpassed, most profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharma, which is difficult to encounter even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas;
I pray that you will explain the true meaning of the Tathāgata.
The two characters "Vajra" (Diamond) are rare in the world; how many practitioners can truly know them?
These thirty-two iron shackles—once they are chewed through, they are themselves the spiritual friend, the Vajra.
"Vajra" means that its self-nature is firm and solid, indestructible throughout eternal kalpas; how much more so is the nature of gold, which is hard and resilient. This gold...
The nature of the vajra is formless and signless; it is rare in the world and difficult to find even in the heavens. Therefore, it is said: "Rare in the world.
At present, all those who practice spend their days in a state of confusion, clinging to signs and seeking [external objects], unaware of the perfect luminosity of the single vajra-nature.
They merely indulge the greed and desire of the six sense faculties that cling to signs. Therefore, it is said: "Cultivation..."
How many people can truly understand this practice? The first two lines state that those who recognize the adamantine nature (*vajra-svabhāva*) are rare.
The latter two lines exhort practitioners to thoroughly chew through and digest this single scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Regarding the term "iron *qié* and *jiǎn*": *qié* refers to an iron blade, while *jiǎn* means a case or sheath. Therefore, it exhorts practitioners to examine [the scripture] closely.
The thirty-two sections of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* are like thirty-two pairs of sharp axes;
each must be chewed and broken down thoroughly. Only if there is someone who can chew them apart may they be called a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Therefore it is said: "To chew them apart is to be a spiritual friend."
The origins of this Dharma assembly are continuous and uninterrupted; yet, failing to maintain right mindfulness, one lets the years and seasons pass in vain.
It is from this that the gathering for preaching the Dharma arises. At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, at that time the World-Honored One, at the hour of eating, put on his robes and took his bowl, entering the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. Having gone through the city begging for alms in due order, he returned to his original place.
When he had finished his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, spread out a seat, and sat down. Because of Subhūti...
Raising the question, it is said: "The origin of this Dharma assembly is without interruption and without rest.

Kāśyapa obtained it through a single smile, which was transmitted directly down to the twenty-eighth patriarch, Bodhidharma. Shenguang obtained it through three prostrations, which was transmitted directly down to the Sixth Patriarch Huineng of Caoxi.
Later, it was transmitted to Nanyue and Mazu, continuing directly down to the present day; hence it is said, "without..."

It ceases without rest. At present, there are certain practitioners who recognize a single "eye" that sees and an "ear" that hears—the caged Buddha-nature; or who know a single True Mind of the Dharma-realm.
They have long perused the scriptures and teachings, accumulating words and characters within their hearts, and then say, "I am capable, I am wise; I have attained enlightenment."

We have arrived, yet we do not maintain a single moment of right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). The *Qingjie lun* (Treatise on Pure Liberation) states: "If you are widely learned and understand everything, how can you reach the center without relying on right mindfulness?
If you clearly realize that right mindfulness is identical to the original ground (*mūla-bhūmi*), why need you utter sounds or expend your breath?
Those who do not maintain right mindfulness in this way merely consume their vegetarian meals in vain and pass their years and seasons to no purpose.
Therefore it is said: "If one does not maintain right mindfulness, one passes the years and seasons in vain. *Tut!* What is right mindfulness?
*Ai!* To eliminate discursive thoughts is itself right mindfulness.
The origin and source from which this Dharma assembly arises: by turning the precious treasury, one attains peace and security;
with a mind free from hindrance, one constantly recollects that the Buddhas are always present before one’s eyes.
These opening words speak of the cause and conditions for the gathering to hear the Dharma; they are the very root of Subhūti’s inquiry.

Source. Presentation of the Verses. It is said that this one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* contains twenty-seven points of doubt and twenty-nine instances of question and answer.
Sometimes the Buddha asks and Subhūti answers; sometimes Subhūti asks and the Buddha answers.
It is like turning over a treasury of jewels. This is when Subhūti asked the World-Honored One: "Good sons and good daughters..."
"One who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: how should they abide? How should they subdue their mind?
The Buddha told Subhūti, "Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.
Son of good family, daughter of good family, one who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide in this way. Thus...
"To subdue the mind—this is precisely the Dharma of Prajñā. Subhūti understood the Buddha’s intent;
as soon as his mind attained inner tranquility, it was said that "by turning the precious treasury, one attains tranquility.
This phrase "turning" refers to the fact that within Subhūti’s mind there is tranquility, yet on the mind there is no obstruction. This, however, is merely a state of indeterminate, dull emptiness.
Therefore it is said: "Constantly, constantly mindful. This "constant mindfulness" means that one cannot be deceived by what is seen with the eyes or heard with the ears;
blue, yellow, red, and white are the very point of realization for the person themselves. Thus it is said: "The Buddhas are at all times present before one's eyes."
The origins of this Dharma assembly are such that all people in the world should be encouraged to practice it while they still can. You may say that you cannot do so;
yet when the great limit of life arrives, no one can save you. When the Buddha-king Yama issues his summons, the three miserable realms of hell will not spare you from receiving their retribution.
The agony is unbearable and knows no end; the agony is unbearable and knows no end.
Our Buddha, the Tathāgata, preached the Dharma for forty-nine years and delivered over three hundred assemblies of sutras;

these were all merely exhortations to people to practice cultivation early on. Yet people of the present age have not yet secured their family fortunes; they are preoccupied with the affection between husband and wife and have not settled worldly affairs.
Their sons and daughters are not yet grown, and they are entangled in myriad matters, saying only, "I am unable to manage it. This is truly a pitiful state of affairs.
The Way. Suddenly, when the great limit of one's life arrives, one is at a loss for what to do at the moment of departure.
Here one takes off the warm cloth shirt; there one puts on the fetal-state robe. Going and coming—when will this ever end?
When will one cross over the bitter sea of birth and death? My Buddha! Outside the Great Iron Ring Mountains, King Yama has a palace.
The palace was sixty yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold nets of bells.
Outside were seven rows of *tāla* trees, and its terraces, palaces, gardens, and groves were all variously beautiful to behold.
Through the king’s own evil karma, molten red copper naturally appeared before him; the palace immediately turned the color of iron. As for the five desires—
All his merit vanished. Having seen this, the King was struck with terror and unease; he immediately fled into the inner quarters.

At that time, the wardens of hell seized King Yama, lifted him high, and dashed him down. They poured molten copper into the King’s mouth, which burned through him in succession until it emerged from below.
The King thought to himself: "In the past, I committed evil deeds, causing me to undergo this suffering. May I—"
Having renounced his own body, he left the household life to enter the path within the Buddha-dharma.
Once he had formed this virtuous resolve, the palace where he resided returned to its former state. When his affairs were concluded, he returned to enjoy himself with his court ladies.
If even the King of Yama is thus, how much more so all sentient beings who undergo suffering? [End of Inscription]
As for "the hook": King Yama dispatches two *mṛtyu* (death) spirits to summon [the deceased]. As for "the hells":
at the bottom of the great ocean, there is a stone named *vajrāgni* (blazing iron), eighty-four thousand *yojana* in length and breadth, and twenty thousand *li* in thickness.
Beneath it lie the eight great hells: the first is named the Great Hell of Revival (*sañjīva*); the second is named the Great Hell of Black Ropes (*kālasūtra*); the third is named...
Together with the great hells, there are four named the Great Hell of Wailing, five named the Great Hell of Great Wailing, six named the Great Hell of Torment,
seven named the Great Hell of Great Torment, and eight named the Avīci Great Hell.
Each successive layer is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and each contains sixteen minor hells.
They are surrounded on all sides. First is the minor hell named Black Cloud Sand; second is the minor hell named Excrement and Filth Mud;
third is the minor hell named Five Forks; fourth is the minor hell named Hunger; fifth is the minor hell named Thirst;
sixth is the minor hell named Pus and Blood; seventh is the minor hell named Single Copper Cauldron; eighth—
1. The minor hell named Many Copper Cauldrons; 2. The minor hell named Iron Millstones;
3. The minor hell named *Piṅgala*; 4. The minor hell named Chicken; 5. The minor hell named River of Ashes; 6.
The minor hell named Cutting and Slicing; 7. The minor hell named Sword-Leaved Forest; 8. The minor hell named Fox and Wolf.
Sixteenth is the minor hell of Cold Ice. As for the "Three Paths," these are the path of hell, the path of hungry ghosts, and the path of animals.
All those who perform karmic actions cannot avoid experiencing them with their own bodies; no one can take their place.
Because they undergo this suffering for five hundred kalpas, it is said: "The agony is difficult to endure, never-ending and without respite."
Subhūti arose and made his request: "Formless and shadowless is one's own Amitābha; yet deluded people do not awaken.

Subhūti—that is, Sūbhūti—arose from his seat amidst the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "How rare!"
"There is a World-Honored One, a Tathāgata who well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas and well entrusts all bodhisattvas.
World-Honored One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide?
How should they subdue their minds? Subhūti then rose from his seat and knelt with his right knee...
He prostrated himself on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and praised the World-Honored One:

"Your body is sixteen feet tall with a complexion like purple-polished gold, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, peerless throughout the three realms. From your mouth you emit eighty-four thousand Dharma gates;
therefore it is said: 'Rare indeed is the World-Honored One! Through the Prajñāpāramitā Dharma, the Tathāgata protects and sustains all beings."

O Bodhisattvas, the Tathāgata, by means of the Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā, entrusts Subhūti and all the great Bodhisattvas to cause practitioners to protect and mind their own persons with the wisdom of prajñā, so that their minds do not become deluded and no false thoughts arise.
Subhūti observes that all sons and daughters of good family are restless and never still in their mindfulness.
With mindfulness continuous and without interruption, how does one abide in the Dharma?
And how does one subdue the mind of deluded conceptualization? The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is just as you have said.
The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas; he well entrusts all bodhisattvas. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain for you."
“You have said it well, son of good family. A son or daughter of good family who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide in this way and thus subdue their mind.
The Tathāgata, observing Subhūti’s profound and lofty inquiry, said, ‘Excellent, excellent! The Buddha addressed Subhūti: ‘It is just as you have spoken.’”
This is the realm beyond kalpas, the space above and beyond; it is the well-guarded heart-mind that you alone have attained.
I call to mind all bodhisattvas; I entrust this well to all bodhisattvas. Listen attentively now; I shall preach the Dharma for you.

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family gives rise to the unsurpassed, true, and correct mind, they should abide in this manner within the Dharma of Prajñā, and in this manner through the Dharma of Prajñā they shall subdue their discursive and deluded mind.
Subhūti said, "So be it, World-Honored One; I wish and desire to hear it. "Subhūti, you should wish that the Buddha explain this extensively, so that you may receive and uphold it."
Those of middling and inferior capacities will all attain enlightenment. This mind of deluded thought is fundamentally not subject to external appearances;
it is neither blue, red, nor white. Therefore, it is said to be "formless and shadowless. This mind of deluded thought does not come from without;
it is truly the Amitābha that has emerged from within oneself. Yongjia said: "The true nature of ignorance..."
This is precisely the Buddha-nature; this illusory, empty body is the Dharma-body. Therefore it is said: "One's own Amitābha.
All deluded people fail to awaken to this meaning; they cling to appearances and do not understand this mind. Thus, they remain lost in succession without ever attaining enlightenment.
Subhūti requests instruction based on his own person: whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he maintains mindfulness of the True Sutra.
If one should step upon the ground of non-arising, then at every step and in every situation, all is perfectly realized.
Subhūti is none other than Subhūti; having arisen, he inquires about the Buddha-dharma. This applies to all practitioners of the path.
"What sutra should be recited? By reciting what sutra does a Bodhisattva abide [in the Dharma], and by reciting what sutra does he subdue his mind of delusive thoughts?

The Buddha said: "By abiding in this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and by subduing his mind of delusive thoughts through this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. This is one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā*.
The *Vajra Sūtra* is not merely something upon paper; rather, it refers to the adamantine nature of gold, which is eternally firm and indestructible, hence it is called "Vajra.
*Prajñā* means wisdom. Wisdom takes skillful means as its merit, while insight (*prajñā*) takes decisive discernment as its function.
*Pāramitā* carries the meaning of reaching the other shore. To realize one's nature and attain deliverance is to ascend to that other shore. [Not yet...]

Those who attain deliverance do so right here on this shore; it is none other than the true nature of the spiritual awakening inherent in every person. Therefore, it is said: "It is originally within the body.

This means that this one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* exists within the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—without interruption and without cessation.
How could it be increased? How could it be diminished? Thus it is said: "In walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, one is mindful of the Truth."
The Sūtra’s first two lines state that this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is present amidst walking, standing, sitting, and reclining;

the latter two lines further require the practitioner to tread upon the ground of non-arising awakening (*anutpattika-dharma-bodhi*). The ritual manual says: "Step by step one treads upon solid ground;
at every turn one bears the void upon one's head. When putting on clothes, one touches the waist and collar; when washing the face, one feels the water.
The bridge of the nose: when climbing up the tree, both hands grasp the branches; when coming down from the pit, both feet touch the ground.
This may be called the total manifestation of perfection at every step and in every moment.
Subhūti arose and requested instruction: "The path one wishes to cultivate is blocked; before one's eyes is a pitch-black void. The six thieves come to cause disturbance. The Buddha said:
"Exert yourself and apply diligent effort! Strike down ignorance, and only then will you attain samādhi. When one dharma is penetrated, all dharmas are penetrated.
When one dharma is penetrated, all dharmas are penetrated."

It is said that Subhūti asked the Tathāgata: "For all practitioners who have not severed their bonds of affection, who have not eliminated the six desires, and who have not yet discarded ignorance, how can they subdue their deluded minds?
Therefore it is said: "Before one's eyes is a pitch-black void; the six thieves come to cause turmoil. My Buddha, you must still instruct the practitioner."
Exert effort. There are five powers: the power of progress, the power of faith, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
If one possesses the power of wisdom, the four things—ignorance, afflictions, craving, and delusive thoughts—are forever extinguished.
One then attains the Samādhi of Non-contention; this is concentration. Therefore it is said: "Kill ignorance dead, and you will immediately attain samādhi."
Concentration. If one attains the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*) and becomes settled therein, the wondrous mind of pure nirvāṇa is revealed;
this is precisely the single true mind of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, when one dharma is penetrated, all dharmas are penetrated.
The Orthodox Tradition of the Mahāyāna: Subduing the Mind. Raising it from the bottom of the sea, it ascends directly to Mount Kunlun.
The Mahāyāna is not the Hīnayāna; the Orthodox Tradition is not a heterodox tradition. The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this manner. "Bodhisattva" is a Sanskrit term; in the Eastern Land [China], it is...
Regarding "the sentient beings with the mind of the Way": *mahā* is a Sanskrit term; in the Eastern Land [China], it is translated as "great. This refers to a Great Bodhisattva.

Although this Great Bodhisattva remains amidst the toils of the mundane world, their mind is always pure. Furthermore, through various skillful means such as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, they transform and guide sentient beings;
thus they are called a "Bodhisattva" (*bodhisattva*). Although they transform sentient beings, their mind is free from grasping or attachment; this is what is meant.
Mahāsattva, to revere all sentient beings is precisely the place where one subdues one's own mind;
therefore it is called "The Orthodox Lineage of the Mahāyāna. Regarding the subsequent two lines, "the ocean floor and Mount Kunlun":
the ocean floor refers to moisture-born beings, while Mount Kunlun refers to Sumeru, the King of Mountains, extending all the way up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.
This refers to all classes of sentient beings: those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from moisture, or those born by transformation;
those with form or without form; those with perception, those without perception, or those neither with nor without perception.
Were it not for those in the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*), I would cause them all to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Those born from eggs have a nature of delusion;
those born from wombs have a nature of habituation; those born from moisture have a nature of following what is false; and those born by transformation have a nature of dogmatic views.

This is the root of the four modes of birth. If one gives rise to a mind that cultivates [the mind], yet does not accord with the principle of formlessness, this is called a deva of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

If one maintains uprightness within the inner mind but does not practice reverence or making offerings, claiming instead that "straightforwardness of mind is itself the Buddha," this is called a deva of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Failing to understand the Middle Way, one perceives with the eyes, hears with the ears, and conceives thoughts with the mind.

Those who are attached to preaching the Dharma, whose mouths speak of the Buddha’s conduct while their minds do not rely upon such practice, are called those of the Heaven of Perception (*saṃjñā-deva*).

Those deluded people who sit in meditation solely to eliminate delusions, who do not study compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, wisdom, or skillful means, and who merely maintain a state of no-mind like wood or stone, are called those of the Heaven of Non-Perception (*asaṃjñā-deva*).
Not being attached to the two perceptions of existence and non-existence, one abides in the Middle Way.
It remains; it is called the Heaven of Non-Non-Ideation (*asaṃjñisattva*). The body is formed by the four aggregates (*skandha*), while the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is realized as empty.
When the mind seeking the principle remains, it is called the Heaven of Neither-Ideation-Nor-Non-Ideation (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

If one attains the emptiness of the five aggregates and all four types of ideation are forgotten, one enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and is thereby extinguished. Therefore, it is said: "Lifting up from the bottom of the sea, one ascends directly to Mount Kunlun."
In the Mahāyāna True Lineage, one must diligently apply effort; those who are deluded seek only outwardly.
The Lion’s Roar ascends to the summit of Mount Sumeru, so that the Māras tremble with fear.
Those who cultivate the Mahāyāna True Lineage must not emulate indolence; they must add valor upon valor and practice with vigor.
Above, apply diligent effort; below, exert yourself directly until death. Suddenly awaken to the true emptiness of the essence of Bodhi.
The entire body is boneless; the whole being is empty space. It stands forth majestically alone, encompassing all phenomena.
There is no mind to be realized, no Way to be accomplished, no Buddha to be made, no Dharma to be preached, and no sentient beings to be saved. The ordinary is itself the sacred.
The sage is none other than the ordinary person; their original nature spontaneously forms a single whole. This is the person of the True Lineage of the Mahāyāna. Thus it is said:

"In the True Lineage of the Mahāyāna, one diligently applies effort. There is only the heterodox lineage of the Hīnayāna, which consists of practicing *zazen* (seated meditation) while engaging in *chan* (meditation).

"Beating the seven-day drum to smelt away demons, reciting sutras and chanting the Buddha's name, bowing to sutras and bowing to Buddhas, seeking birth in the Buddha-land, or aspiring to be born in the heavens of dhyāna—such deluded people seek only outwardly.
As for the 'lion,' it is a metaphor for those who follow the authentic tradition of the Mahayana.
When the roar of the golden-maned lion comes, all wild foxes are utterly distressed. [At the summit of] Mount Sumeru...
This refers to the gods of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.

When this person of the True Lineage of the Mahāyāna lets out a single roar, all the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, as well as the Māras who transform others, are utterly struck with such terror that their gallbladders tremble and their hearts grow cold.
Therefore it is said: "He strikes the Māras so that their gallbladders tremble in competition."
The True Source of the Mahāyāna: Contemplating in stillness, my heart is struck with awe. Having cast off the maladies of greed and anger, I examine the field of the mind and find it tranquil.
Buddha! Wisdom is the universal radiance; once the drifting clouds have vanished, the mirror of Xuanyuan is revealed. Before the Platform of Perfect Enlightenment, the myriad dharmas are empty.
Before the Platform of Perfect Enlightenment, the myriad dharmas are empty.
A follower of the Mahāyāna orthodox tradition, dwelling in a pure and secluded place, contemplates the words of the Tathāgata and his heart is struck with awe and trepidation.
The Buddha said: "In this way, although one liberates immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain liberation.
Those who are 'liberated' are, in fact, those who have attained emancipation. Why is this? Subhūti..."
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva.
The buddha-nature of sentient beings is fundamentally without difference; it is because of the presence of these four marks that they do not enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
To possess these four marks is to be a sentient being; to lack these four marks is to be liberated. Upon awakening, one is a sentient being.
This is the Buddha. As for the four marks: when a deluded person relies on their wealth, learning, or noble lineage to look down upon all others, this is called the mark of self (*ātman*).

Although one practices the conduct of a Buddha, if the notion of "self" and "other" is not eliminated, this is called the mark of persons (*pudgala*). To attribute good deeds to oneself is [the mark of attachment].

To direct evil deeds toward others is called the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*). To seek rebirth in the heavens, to vow to be born in the Western Land, or for the mind to crave long life is called the mark of a self (*jīvaka-nimitta*). To possess these four marks is to be a sentient being; thus it is said:
"Within purity, the calculating mind itself is startled. If one is a person of the True School of the Mahāyāna, they must first eliminate their own greed and anger.
The disease of ignorance must be treated with the true medicine of precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
At every moment, one must examine whether the field of one’s own mind is pure. My Buddha, if you attain the radiance of wisdom, its flames shall shatter former darkness.
The drifting clouds are afflictions; the mirror of Xuanyuan is the full moon. When the drifting clouds of affliction have completely receded, the [true nature] is revealed.
The single wheel of the moon of original nature emerges; thus it is said: "When the floating clouds have completely retreated, the mirror of Xuanyuan appears.
Before the platform of Great Vehicle Perfect Enlightenment, all phenomena are empty; originally there is not a single thing. The *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* states:

"When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the voids of the ten directions are entirely dissolved. Therefore it is said: "Before the platform of Perfect Enlightenment, the myriad..."
The dharmas are empty;
wondrous practice is non-abiding. The divine spirits all provide protection; one’s own numinous light spontaneously advances.
This profound and wondrous practice is fundamentally without attachment or dwelling. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva regarding the dharmas should be without...
That which is abiding is precisely non-abiding in form, sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, and mental phenomena when practicing giving. Therefore it is said: "Sublime practice is without abiding.
Wherever there is a person whose sublime practice is without abiding, that place is as if a Buddha were present;
for this reason, all spiritual deities provide protection. Why is this? If a Bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, their merit and virtue are...
It is inconceivable. When a Bodhisattva practices giving, their mind is free from seeking;
the merit thus obtained is as immeasurable as the empty space of the ten directions. "Bù" (布) means universal, and "shī" (施) means to scatter.

One who is able to universally scatter and exhaust the delusive thoughts and habitual tendencies within the mind—afflictions, ignorance, pride, arrogance, and valor—is one who has nothing accumulated.
This is true giving. Although possessing the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, one does not cling to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects;
this is true giving. The mind is constantly pure, realizing that all phenomena are empty and quiescent, and internally eliminating greed and attachment.
Externally setting aside self and person, when seeing others commit evil, one does not perceive their faults;
practicing according to the teachings with a mind free of subject and object—this is true giving. Practicing in this way is giving that does not dwell on signs;
its merit is inconceivable. The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "What do you think? Can the empty space of the eastern direction be measured?"
"Is it measurable? Subhūti understood the meaning. "The space of the eastern direction is boundless and limitless;

therefore, he said, 'No, World-Honored One. The Buddha again called to Subhūti: "As for the space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—is it conceivable?
Subhūti understood the meaning. "The space of the ten directions has no boundaries or limits; therefore, he said, 'No.'"
"Furthermore, World-Honored One," [Subhūti said]. The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The merit of a bodhisattva’s giving without abiding in signs is likewise such that it cannot be measured or conceived. Thus he instructed Subhūti: "A bodhisattva should simply abide as taught.
This means that one should simply abide in signless giving. An ancient said: "Beginning from the moment of disciplined mindfulness..."
The merit of this must surely bring about the ground of non-action (*wuwei*); this is precisely the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva. Therefore it is said:
"The numinous light of one's own self happens to advance;
wondrous practice dwells nowhere—how rare in the world! Who knows this mysterious and subtle news?"

Opening a single eye of the heavenly vision, one cannot purchase such a person of wondrous practice who dwells nowhere—even with ten thousand taels of gold. They do not dwell in the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
they do not dwell in the east, the west, the south, the north, the zenith, or the nadir.
Do not dwell in heaven; do not dwell in hell. Do not dwell in Chan meditation; do not dwell in seated zazen.

Do not dwell in seven-day retreats; do not dwell in the smelting of demons. Do not dwell in burning incense; do not dwell in lighting candles. Do not dwell in reciting the Buddha’s name or reading the sutras.
All things abide nowhere. Therefore, this wondrous practice has no dwelling place; it is rare in the world.
This profound and subtle communication—that which exhausts empty space and pervades the Dharma-realm—is what principle is that? Thus it is said: "Who knows this profound and subtle communication?
If you obtain an enlightened master who pierces open for you a single eye that penetrates both heaven and earth, you will clearly behold the eternal...
Throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one perceives ten thousand billion Buddha-fields;
one personally beholds countless Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all unified within a single Dharma-body.
Such a realization is something that even ten million ounces of gold could not purchase.
Sublime conduct is non-abiding; delusive thoughts of greed and anger are completely swept away. Cease the rising of arrogance; the deluded mind cannot be concealed.
The Buddha and the Māra kings are all executed. The monkey is captured and shackled to the Cool and Refreshing Tree.
There is more than enough joy in this sovereign ease and leisure. Sovereign ease and leisure—there is more than enough joy.
A person of wondrous practice who abides nowhere is not like a cripple leaning against a wall or a blind man relying on a Buddha to lead him across.
Such a person of wondrous practice who abides nowhere relies upon nothing at all. As the ritual manual says:
"The wondrous essence is fundamentally without location; throughout the entire body, how could there be any further trace? Therefore, it is wondrous.

Practice without abiding. If one is a person who cultivates wondrous conduct, all delusive thoughts—greed, anger, arrogance, and bellicosity—as well as deceiving the mind and obscuring the self, must be completely swept away without remainder. Therefore it is said:
"The deceptive mind cannot remain; my Buddha. If one succeeds in sweeping these away completely, the Demon King will surely seize him; therefore it is said: "The Demon King."
They are all executed. Furthermore, one must take the mind-monkey and the will-horse and lock them upon the cool, shadowless tree, not permitting the blazing fire of the sun to reach them.
Thus it is said: "Locked upon the cool tree, one attains the joy of spontaneous freedom in abundance.
*Duh!* For all practitioners of the Way, what is it that cannot be locked? *Ya!* It is because they do not recognize the pure.
The cool, shadowless tree is instead scorched by the blazing fire of the sun, which burns through the Tathāgata’s locks of precept,
concentration, and wisdom. Thus, having failed to restrain the heart-monkey and the mind-horse, one wanders aimlessly from home, unable to attain liberation.
Seeing according to reality is like a flash of lightning: from top to bottom, it is luminously penetrating and unified as one.
Suchness, the wondrous principle of true reality, constitutes the authentic vision. The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "What do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of physical marks? Subhūti understood the intent: he possesses no such marks; how [could he be seen otherwise]?
Seeking form within the [five] aggregates, one finds that this physical form has been non-existent from the very beginning; therefore, he replied, "No, World-Honored One.
One cannot perceive the Tathāgata by means of physical characteristics. Why is this? The physical characteristics spoken of by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not physical characteristics."
The physical body (*rūpakāya*) is the characteristic; the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is the nature. All good and evil arise from the Dharma-body, not from the physical body.
If the Dharma-body performs evil, the physical body will not produce good; if the Dharma-body performs good, the physical body will not produce evil.
Ordinary beings perceive only the physical body and do not perceive the Dharma-body; therefore, the answer is that the characteristics of the body are themselves non-existent.
[Regarding] marks (*lakṣaṇa*). The Buddha told Subhūti: "All marks whatsoever are entirely false and illusory. Before a single thought has arisen, the afflictions (*kleśa*) have already begun;
to be deluded and abandon one's original nature is entirely false and illusory. Therefore, they are like a flash of lightning.
If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. Because the Tathāgata wishes to manifest the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), he speaks of all..."

Characteristics are false and unreal; to see them as such is to see the Dharmakāya. When the principle is thus realized, the upper and lower become transparently clear and are forged into a single whole.
To see reality as it truly is, the original truth is simply present within one’s own single thought-moment.
In the four intermediate directions, above, and below, there is nothing that does not encompass [the light]; the great earth, mountains, and rivers are all entirely gold.
This is seeing according to reality as it truly is; it is not a false view nor that of the Hīnayāna.

When a person of the Hīnayāna contemplates the realms of the four directions, they may see blue light or red light, or they may see golden light or white light, or they may see returning light in circular forms.
Light. Or one may see blue lotuses and red lotuses; or see golden lotuses and white lotuses; or see golden terraces and pavilions;
or see Amitābha Buddha filling the ten directions; or see Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta constantly coming to receive and guide one.
Any such perceived appearances are all false appearances. As the ritual manual states: "Within the Eye of the True Dharma, nothing can be obtained."
If one is a person who sees according to reality as it is, and sees all marks as being no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
Seeing yellow flowers, one faces the yellow flowers; seeing green bamboo, one faces the green bamboo. A monk asked Dàlóng, "The physical body perishes;
what is the firm, solid Dharmakāya? Dàlóng said, "Mountain flowers bloom like brocade; the mountain stream flows."
It is as clear and deep as indigo. One who attains such a vision is said to possess the "true vision according to reality.

As for the person of original nature (*benlai ren*), they can take a single blade of grass and make it the sixteen-foot golden body, and take that sixteen-foot golden body and make it a single blade of grass.

Therefore it is said: "The true vision according to reality sees the person of original nature. This person of original nature resides right upon the face of the present person, before their very eyes.
That which is seen with the eyes, heard with the ears, smelled by the nose, spoken by the mouth, grasped by the hands, walked by the feet, and deliberated by the mind—
all these reside solely within the single thought-moment of the person. This enlightened, true nature of the person cannot be covered by heaven,
cannot be supported by earth, cannot be harmed by yin and yang, cannot be enslaved by the five elements, and cannot be affected by ghosts or spirits.
It can be constrained; even the kalpa-fire cannot harm it. Therefore it is said: "In the four intermediate directions, above, and below, there is nothing that can contain it.
If one realizes that the entire earth is a single sixteen-foot golden body, it is said: "The great earth, mountains, and rivers are all gold."

Seeing things as they truly are, the ten evils and eight perversions are present before one’s eyes, and their luminous essence is fully manifest. For those of delusion and many discursive thoughts, the Buddha says:
apply even greater diligence in practice. Through long-term effort, it will naturally become a single whole. Once the lump of clay is shattered, there is no need for further practice;
once the lump of clay is shattered, there is no need for further practice.
Why is it that this person who perceives things according to reality and truth cannot return to their home? Alas!

Because of the ten evils and the eight heterodoxies, one cannot return to one's home. As for the ten evils, they consist of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, which are divided into ten; first, the body...
There are three evil deeds of the body: sexual misconduct, killing, and stealing. There are three evils of the mind: greed, hatred, and delusion. There are four evils of the mouth:
false speech, frivolous chatter, harsh words, and divisive speech. As for the eightfold wrong path: the conceit of "I" and "mine" is Mount Sumeru, and the perverse mind is the ocean water.
Afflictions are the waves; poisonous harm is the evil dragons; falsehood is the ghosts and spirits; worldly toil is the fish and turtles; greed and anger are the hells;
and ignorance is the realm of animals. If one can eliminate the notion of self and others, Mount Sumeru will topple.

Depart from the deviant mind. Thirst for the seawater [of existence] ceases; afflictions become waveless; ripples subside and poisonous harms are forgotten. Evil dragons are cut off; falsehoods vanish;
spirits and ghosts are extinguished and the dust of toil disperses. Fish and turtles cease; greed and anger are forgotten. Hells are extinguished and ignorance severed; the animal realm is cut off.
Therefore, although the ten evils and eight deviances are before one's eyes, if there is someone who recognizes their own [nature], [they will not be bound by them].
One’s own radiance does not fail to penetrate the ten evils and eight perversions.
*Du!* Do you wish to see this radiance? *Ei!* Listen to my ten-character verse: The eyes emit light, capable of illuminating blue, yellow, red, and white.
The ears emit light, capable of hearing good and bad sounds. The nose emits light, capable of perceiving fragrance and stench. The tongue emits light...
Discussing the profound mystery, he universally delivers all sentient beings. His body emits light; he knows cold and heat, and can discern hunger and satiety.

His mind emits light; he knows high and low. His transformations are manifold; his entire body is transparently radiant. Emitting light that shakes the earth, he radiates brilliance throughout the Dharma-realm.
Standing alone as the Honored One, the light of his glory is thus fully manifested. In these present times...

All deluded and ignorant people fail to recognize their own inner radiance; their discursive thoughts are numerous, their attachment to loved ones is unbroken, and their ego-clinging is not eliminated.
For this reason, they harbor many delusions and thoughts, saying, "My Buddha is currently in another land. This is the current state of those who follow the teachings.
I earnestly exhort all practitioners to cultivate with diligence and valor, further engaging in inquiry, seeking out an enlightened master, and requesting their seal of certification (*mudrā*).
Once the authenticity of the master is certified, through the long-term application of the "Bird Path" (*vīthi*) practice, one will suddenly hear that person and dharma are both forgotten;
with a single "cluck" of the throat, they become a single seamless whole. Therefore it is said: "The work of long duration... from oneself.
Yet it forms a single mass. If one wishes to form this single mass, one must break the clay ball.
Should there be someone who can smash it to pieces, all matters will be concluded; thus it is said: "Smash the lump of clay and there is no need for Zen study."
Right faith is rare and extraordinary. Like the bellowing of an iron ox, it causes Mount Sumeru to tremble and collapse, and causes malevolent spirits and demons to flee.
To practice right faith by cultivating it within the mind—such a person is the most supreme and rare of all. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, are there any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases, will give rise to true faith?"
"No, Subhūti. This Dharma of Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
How could ordinary people of the final age, whose wisdom is meager and inferior, believe and enter into these chapters and verses of the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra* upon hearing them? The Buddha said:
"Subhūti, do not speak in such a manner. After the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit."

The True Dharma shall endure for one thousand years. During the first five hundred years, liberation shall be the primary essence; during the latter five hundred years, meditative concentration shall be the primary essence.
Those who heard this Prajñāpāramitā dharma while the Tathāgata was in the world did not consider it difficult;

however, in the final five hundred years and even into the period of the Semblance Dharma, all shall practice meditative concentration, yet they will neither attain meditative concentration nor attain liberation.
Regarding these words and phrases of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, those who are able to give rise to faith and take them as true—
know that such persons have not merely made offerings to the Buddha in one lifetime, nor in two lifetimes, nor in three, four, or five lifetimes.
Thus they plant roots of goodness. Having already made offerings to Buddhas for immeasurable tens of millions of lifetimes, what is meant by "planting various roots of goodness"?
To describe this briefly below: it refers to making offerings with a single mind to the Buddhas and following their teachings;
[making offerings] to Bodhisattvas, spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), teachers, preceptors, virtuous elders, eminent monks, and fathers.
The Noble Mother has always practiced respectful conduct, making offerings and obediently following her instructions. She never contravened their wishes.

Toward all sentient beings who are poor and suffering, she gave rise to a heart of compassion and mercy, never feeling contempt or weariness. Whatever they required, she bestowed as charity according to her capacity.
Toward the sentient beings of the six realms, she did not inflict harm, nor did she deceive, despise, disparage, or humiliate them.
They do not ride them, nor do they whip them; they do not eat their flesh, but always act for their benefit. This is called planting various roots of goodness.
Now, those who hear these words and phrases of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and give rise to pure faith for even a single thought-moment—therefore, such right faith is rare.
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, the Tathāgata fully knows all such sentient beings who possess this pure faith."
They all see it. These sentient beings have attained such a Dharma and immeasurable, boundless merit. Why is this?
Because these sentient beings no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span.
There is no characteristic of the dharma of prajñā, nor is there any non-attainment of the characteristic of the dharma of prajñā.

Although such a person practices prajñā, their mind does not dwell in the view of emptiness. Why is this? If these sentient beings grasp at characteristics within their minds, they become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
If they grasp at the characteristic of the dharma of prajñā, they likewise become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
"O Āyuṣmat, why is this? If one grasps at the characteristics of dharmas that are not Prajñāpāramitā, one is then attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Therefore, one should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at non-dharmas. These two phrases mean that grasping is neither [correct] nor [acceptable]."
It is neither grasped nor negated. For this reason, the Tathāgata has often said to you bhikṣus:
"Understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the parable of the raft. Even the Dharma should be abandoned, let alone these dharmas such as rebirth in heaven.
Therefore it is said: "Right faith is rare. One who cultivates right faith is likened to an iron ox; they do not acknowledge human sentiments. *Āo*.
With a single roar, all phenomena are revealed as empty; even Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is toppled.
Throughout the three realms, the eighteen Brahma heavens, and the twenty-five states of existence—including the realm of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods—the Māra kings find no place to rest.
Thus it is said that Mount Sumeru is shaken and toppled, and the malevolent spirits flee in all directions.
The rare and wondrous Dharma of Right Faith is transmitted; In a single thought, without deviation, it pervades the great chiliocosm.
Though the Yellow River flows in nine bends and turns upside down, Throughout heaven and across the earth, it remains a single perfect orb.
One who cultivates right faith does not rely on eloquence of tongue, nor on the treading of feet; they depend entirely upon applying effort within the ground of the mind.
Exert yourself in the ground of the mind and completely cast aside worldly affairs. The Buddha told Subhūti: "For what reason?
If these sentient beings take up signs with their minds, or seek the Western Land, or seek rebirth in the heavens, or seek to become humans in future lives..."

This constitutes attachment to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span. If one grasps at the characteristics of dharmas, thinking, "I have attained the dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā*," one is then attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.

If one grasps at the characteristics of non-dharmas, thinking, "I am not practicing the dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā*," one is then attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span. Therefore, one should not grasp at dharmas.

One should not grasp at what is not the Dharma. When a practitioner recognizes this illness and clearly understands this principle, it is the wondrous method for transcending birth and escaping death.
Therefore it is said: "Right faith is rare; the wondrous Dharma is transmitted. But what is being transmitted?
In the past, the World-Honored One transmitted the treasury of the true Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*, to Mahākāśyapa;
Kāśyapa obtained it through a single smile. Continuing down to the twenty-eighth patriarch, Bodhidharma, he obtained it through three prostrations.
Continuing down to the sixth patriarch, Huineng, all were of right faith and the wondrous Dharma, which is called "a single thought-moment" (*ekakṣaṇa*). Nowadays, there are those who are deluded...
People, simply hold up one phrase: "Namo Amitābha Buddha. Contemplate it for a single thought-moment. How can this encompass the entire great trichiliocosm?
If you err by even a hair's breadth, you will lose the mark by a thousand li. I shall now speak directly: that which is called "one thought" is precisely non-thought;
non-thought is precisely prajñā. As the Heart Sūtra says: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time rely upon..."
Regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, it is said: "Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Alas! What is this Dharma of Prajñāpāramitā?
It requires the complete perfection of the Prajñā-dharma, such that not even a single point of the conscious mind remains.
In this way, a single thought-moment, without deviation, pervades the great trichiliocosm. The Yellow River with its nine bends flows into the Celestial River;
its waters always flow eastward, and for this reason the rivers, lakes, seas, and oceans of this world do not dry up. The ritual manual says:

"Wherever there is water in a thousand rivers, there is the moon in each. If the waters of the Yellow River were to reverse their course and flow back upstream, there would be no water left in the world.
As soon as one recognizes the meaning of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West—water in the long river, the moon in the sky—ha ha!
Truly, it is like being unaware that within the bright day and clear blue sky there are so many who wander lost with their eyes wide open. Thus it is said:
"The Yellow River of nine bends flows backward; throughout heaven and across the earth, a single orb is full."

Right faith is rare and extraordinary. Greed for fame and profit is like a flower upon the water or a bubble. Before your achievements in fame and office are complete, do not seek to contend with one another over the Buddha;
turn your heads back quickly and early. When the fire burns your eyebrows, you must save your head.
In one day of impermanence, all matters cease; in one day of impermanence, there is nothing left to do.
"Correct" refers to the essence; it is propriety. "Trustworthy" refers to sincerity; it is gravity. If there is propriety without trustworthiness, the intention will surely not be sincere.
If there is trustworthiness without propriety, the mind will surely not be substantial. When both are fully present, they may be called correct trustworthiness.
A person who cultivates correct trustworthiness perceives fame and profit as well as the craving for sensory pleasures to be like bubbles floating on water—swiftly arising and swiftly extinguishing.
How could these be considered permanent? Therefore, fame and profit are like greedy flowers upon water bubbles.
Before one’s achievements are realized, do not harbor arrogance, conceit, or engage in disputes over right and wrong.
Thus it is said: "Do not engage in mutual strife; my Buddha, quickly turn back your head. Do not wait until you face peril to practice, for it will be too late. Listen to my verse: One.
A single lamp illuminates the night chamber; one goes up to bed, stripping off socks and shoes. At the third watch of the night, one follows dreams away;
who knows whether dawn will come or not? Therefore, it is like when the eyebrows are already burning, one only then reaches for the head to save it.
An ancient said: "When impermanence arrives in a single day, one only then knows that one is but a person in a dream. Of all things, nothing can be taken away;
only karma follows one's body. Therefore it is said: "In a single day of impermanence, all affairs cease."
There is nothing attained and nothing taught; this is truly difficult to extinguish. If there is even the slightest bit [of grasping], it is like a speck of dust in the eye.
When the essence itself is empty and still, there is no thing to be attained. All that exists as verbal expression is but deceptive speech.
The Buddha called out to Subhūti: "What do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"

"Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma? Subhūti replied, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed dharma that can be attained, nor is there any that can be preached.

That which is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed perfect enlightenment) likewise has no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata could preach. Therefore, there is neither attainment nor preaching."
Subhūti said: "For what reason? All the dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are ungraspable; the dharmas of the Tathāgata cannot be spoken.
When the Tathāgata speaks the Dharma, if one recites it with the mouth but does not practice it with the mind, that is not the Dharma.

If one recites it with the mouth and practices it with the mind, that is indeed neither-dharma-nor-non-dharma. To discuss it in such a way is merely indeterminate, stubborn emptiness—the livelihood of ghosts."
Why is this? All noble and holy ones are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Because the faculties and natures of the three vehicles differ, their understandings are not the same, and their insights vary in depth; thus, there are distinctions. When the Buddha speaks of the unconditioned dharma, he refers to this.
This is precisely non-abiding. Non-abiding is precisely signlessness. Signlessness is precisely non-arising. Non-arising is precisely non-extinction. Ha!
Do you wish to see that which is neither arising nor extinguishing? Call out "Zhang San! and he responds with "Yes. Call out "Li Si!
and he responds with "Haha. This is indeed liberation and Buddha-nature in its true ground; therefore, it is truly difficult to extinguish. At this present time...

There are those who practice with a sense of equality, yet harbor deluded thoughts that the Buddha will come to save them, or that at the time of their death, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta will welcome and lead them to the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
Or they may seek rebirth in the heavens of dhyāna, or the realm of desire, or the four formless concentrations, or seek to become human in a future life.
For this reason, although gold dust is precious, when it falls into the eye it becomes but a speck of dust.

Therefore it is said: If there is even the slightest speck of dust clinging to the eye, one will find neither attainment nor the path of non-attainment and non-explanation. Apply the whip and advance further to cultivate before you;
at all times raise [the mind] and do not let it go, until you reach the far shore of *pāra*.
"Neither attaining nor speaking": it is not that there is attainment, nor is it that there is speaking.
If one were to speak of attainment, fundamentally there are no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind; there are no wondrous marks of blue, yellow, red, or white—what would there be to attain?
If one speaks, the Buddha-dharma is neither on paper nor upon the tongue—what would there be to say? Thus spoke the ancients.
It is said: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time have their mouths hung upon the wall; the patriarchs of successive generations have tied their tongues for seven years.
This is the very headway of the true path. If you wish to cultivate a person who has reached this headway of the true path, you must apply the whip and advance further.
With supreme courage upon courage, press forward in your cultivation. Do not emulate those who are indolent, for they have no end to their suffering.
At every moment and at every instant, maintain right mindfulness; do not let it slip away. In this way, you will reach the further shore of *pāramitā*.
If you err even for a single moment, you will be seen through by ghosts and spirits, who will seize you and take you to the underworld.

At that time, it was not that the enemy could not find a teacher; it was not that the teacher would not speak. It was simply that you yourself were unwilling to rely [on the teaching]. There is neither attainment nor speech.
The mysterious and wondrous secret of the Buddhas and Patriarchs coming from the West made Mahākāśyapa laugh until he collapsed. Shen Guang severed his arm.
The Buddha skillfully manifested the three carts to universally save sentient beings. Depart from the three realms as soon as possible. Recite the name of Amitābha!
Return! Return! Mind Amitābha well and return!
The path of neither attainment nor discourse is the wondrous secret of the Buddhas and Patriarchs’ coming from the West.
In days of yore, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One flashed his blue-lotus eyes as a sign; yet among the fourfold assembly, there was no one who could comprehend it.
This was the hidden intent. Only Mahākāśyapa gave a single smile. The Buddha said: "My Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, I entrust to you.
You must perpetually propagate it and never let it be interrupted. He spoke in verse: "The Dharma is originally no-dharma; No-dharma is also dharma.
Now, when I transmit no-dharma, In all dharmas, how have they ever been dharma? Mahākāśyapa...
Bodhidharma passed away on Mount Jizu and entered the samādhi of cessation.

Later, when he arrived in the West and met Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, the Emperor asked, "I have built monasteries, transcribed scriptures, and provided meals for monks beyond counting; what merit do these deeds bring? The Master replied:
“There is no merit at all, Your Majesty. The Emperor asked, “Why is there no merit? The Master replied, “This is merely a small fruit of the human and celestial realms, a cause of outflow (āsrava).
It follows the body like a shadow; though it exists, it is not real. The Emperor asked, “What, then, is true merit?”
The Master said, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence and function are empty and still. Such merit is not to be sought through worldly means.
The Emperor asked again, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? The Master said, "Vast emptiness—there is no sage here. The Emperor said, "Who is it that faces me?
The Master said, "I do not know. The Emperor did not understand. The Master, sensing that their karmic conditions were not in accord, crossed the river and took up residence elsewhere.
At Shaolin Monastery, he sat facing a wall all day long. A monk named Shen Guang came to visit him morning and evening, standing in the snow until it reached his knees.
The Master took pity on him and asked, "Standing so long in the snow, what do you seek? Guang replied with tears of grief:
"I only pray that the Master, out of compassion, will open the gate of ambrosia. The Master said, "The wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort throughout vast kalpas;

one must be able to perform what is difficult to perform and endure what is difficult to endure. How could it be attained with small virtue or small wisdom, or with a frivolous mind or a conceited mind?"
Baoguang immediately took up a knife and severed his own arm. The Master, recognizing him as a vessel for the Dharma, said:

"When the Buddhas first sought the Way, they forgot their very forms for the sake of the Dharma. Since you have now severed your arm before me, your request may well be granted. He gave him the name Huike. Huike said:
"May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas? Huik'e asked. The Master said, "The Dharma-seal is not obtained from another.
Huik'e said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to grant me peace. The Master said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall grant you peace.
Huik'e said, "I have searched for my mind, but it cannot be found. The Master said, "I have now granted you peace. This, in the end, was precisely the state of neither attainment nor explanation.

This is a sublime expedient. My skillful means involve manifesting three vehicles: the sheep cart, the deer cart, and the ox cart. These are metaphors for the Śrāvaka vehicle, as the capacities and roots of beings differ in magnitude;
thus, I exhort practitioners through these skillful means to manifest the three vehicles and deliver sentient beings, so that they may swiftly escape the triple world.
As for the triple world: it consists of the ten heavens of the desire realm and the [form realm]...
The realms: the eighteen Brahma heavens and the formless realms, the four heavens of emptiness—these three realms.

All the devas therein exist within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). As the ancients said: "As long as one has not transcended beyond the three realms, one remains entirely within the five aggregates. As for these five aggregates:
These are precisely form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. People practicing these times do not recognize this principle. As the common saying goes:
"When the mind is stirred and a thought arises, Heaven and Earth know it all. How can I be taught to escape this?
*Ei!* If one does not stir a thought, one is immediately outside the three realms. The Tathāgata said: "Right now, you are always outside the three realms; it is simply..."
Exhausting all that is unconditioned, they depart from the Sahā world. Such persons as these delight in mindful recollection of their own Amitābha, returning to him.
Born according to the Dharma, they are without marks and without form. Those within the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence are all deluded beings.
The Dharma upon which all Buddhas rely is entirely produced from this single fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:

"What do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift—considering one four-continent world, one sun and moon, one King of Mountains, Mount Sumeru, and the four great oceans..."
One world-system consists of each of these [four continents] multiplied by one thousand, forming a small chiliocosm.

When such small chiliocosms are further multiplied by one thousand, there are ten billion four great continents, ten billion suns and moons, ten billion Sumeru kings of mountains, and ten billion four great oceans;
this constitutes a medium chiliocosm. When the medium chiliocosm is multiplied by one thousand, there are ten trillion [world-systems], each being a great trichiliocosm.
If one were to take a trichiliocosm and give it as a gift using the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and so forth—would the merit obtained by that person be great?

Subhūti, understanding the intent [of the Buddha], replied that it would indeed be very much, for such is the cause of the outflowing (āsrava) blessings and rewards of gods and humans. Why is this? Because that merit is not [merit].

Merit and purity—therefore the Tathāgata says that such merit is vast. That which is of no benefit whatsoever is, according to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the cultivation of one's own original nature; by this one is not born into the evil realms.
This is called the nature of merit, as the Tathāgata has said. Furthermore, if there should be someone who receives and upholds this sūtra, even for four [lines]...
To explain even a single verse or phrase of this for others brings merit far superior to that.
Indeed, while the merit from bestowing the seven treasures upon the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system is finite, why is this so?
Subhūti, it is because all Buddhas and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* dharma of all Buddhas all proceed from this single scroll of the *Vajracchedikā*.
The Sūtra says: This sūtra is not the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* written upon paper; it is the Vajra of one's own fundamental nature (*prakṛti*).
From this essence, function arises; one must constantly maintain awakening and illumination. When the mind of awakening and illumination moves, it is the movement of all Buddhas.
One must fear that awakening and illumination may be delayed; for the Dharma of the Buddhas' *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is entirely born from awakening and illumination.
Therefore, it is born from the Dharma. The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "That which is called 'Buddha-dharma' exists only where there is a mind of attachment;
it is not the Buddha-dharma. All words and phrases are like a signpost or a finger.

One relies on the signpost to take hold of an object, and relies on the finger to perceive the moon. The moon is neither the signpost nor the finger; one merely relies on the sutra to grasp [the truth]."
The Dharma is not the scripture. The scriptural text can be seen with the physical eye; the Dharma, however, can be seen only with the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
If one lacks the wisdom-eye, one sees only the text and does not see the Dharma. If one does not see the Dharma, one does not understand the Buddha’s intent.
Without understanding the Buddha’s intent, even if one recites this scripture ten thousand times over, one will not attain liberation. Therefore, it is said: "It is signless" (*animitta*).
It is formless. At present, all practitioners do not recognize that they themselves possess a scroll of the True Diamond Sutra;
thus, they remain buried within the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence. For this reason, those in the four modes of birth and the six realms are all deluded beings.
According to the Dharma, give rise to it and apply yourself diligently; The clay ox draws water up to Mount Kunlun.
Let the rotten wood and stubborn stone cease their dead-sitting; Mountains and rivers are fully revealed as the body of the Dharma King.
The *Heart Sūtra* says: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Luo. Samyak-saṃbodhi. From the Buddhas of antiquity, all have emerged from this sutra.
If you wish to transcend the three realms, you must apply diligent effort. Therefore, according to the Dharma, one should skillfully apply effort.
As for the "clay ox": when a clay ox draws water, how can its physical form be seen? Since there is no physical form, it manifests as the person themselves. As for "Kunlun": one must...
Mount Sumeru is like a person of the Supreme Vehicle (Ekayāna), standing alone in majestic brilliance, encompassing the three realms;
hence it is said: "The clay ox draws water up to Mount Kunlun. Nowadays, there is a certain class of practitioners who...
Sitting in meditation and entering samādhi is like withered wood or stubborn stone; it is a state devoid of activity. Therefore, withered wood and stubborn stone rest in death-like stillness.

Observe that which sets the stars and constellations in motion, that which moves the sun and moon, that which brings forth wind and rain, that which causes frost and snow to fall, that which brings spring growth and summer flourishing, that which harvests in autumn and stores away in winter, and that which causes flowers to bloom.
Flowers wither; water flows and wind moves; clouds rise and birds fly. Hehe! It turns out that mountains and rivers fully reveal the body of the Dharma King.
Born according to the Dharma, strive diligently in Zen meditation and apply yourself with effort. Obeying the decree of the Empty King, he opens the cave of delusive thoughts.
The Buddha first dwells in the City of Nirvana, establishes his headquarters, and arranges his precious fortress.
Having captured the Demon King, peace is secured; having captured the Demon King, peace is secured.
According to the Dharma of Prajñāpāramitā, those who practice must truly exert themselves in the study of Chan.
"Chan" means purity. If one can exert oneself in the study of Chan, only through purity will one realize one's nature; therefore it is said:
"It is well to exert oneself in the study of Chan and apply diligent effort. "Emptiness-King" refers to the wondrous essence of true emptiness. Since this has been upheld...
Obey the command of the King of Emptiness; do not think that mere intellectual recognition is sufficient for complete understanding.
If one speaks of "self," it is impossible to recognize the essence of true emptiness and bodhi without removing the defilements of the mind.
If one truly realizes the nature of birth and death, one must strike down these myriad thoughts and calculations regarding others. Therefore, it is said: "Strike!"
He opened the Huisi Cave. "My Buddha," he said, "Nirvana is not death; it is non-arising and non-extinction.
'Non-arising' means that the self and personhood do not arise. 'Non-extinction' means that enlightened awareness does not cease.
Therefore, those who first dwell in the Citadel of Nirvana and form the twelve military camps are those who govern the soldiers and civilians of the world and serve [the Dharma]."
By the decree of the King of Emptiness, the twelve *tuán-yíng* (military camps) were dispatched to their original lords and stationed at the Precious Fortress (*bǎo-zhài*).
Once everything was settled and the officials had captured the Demon King, the world finally attained peace.
*Duō!* It is these twelve *tuán-yíng*. *Yī!* They are not in Beijing; they are right here. They are none other than these two eyes and these two...
One pair of ears, one nose, one mouth, one body, one mind, two hands, and a pair of feet—these are called the Twelve Imperial Guard Battalions.
Therefore it is said: "Seize the Demon King, and peace is assured."
One mark is no-mark. Deluded people merely insist on duality; they take two five-hundred coins and treat them as a single thousand.
This very "one mark" is, from the beginning, formless—the pure, void, and wondrous Way. It leaves no trace. The Buddha called out, "Subhūti, what do you think?
Can a srotāpanna (stream-enterer) give rise to such a thought of prajñā as 'I have attained the fruit of a srotāpanna'?"
"Is it the fruit of srotāpanna? Subhūti, the Sanskrit term *srotāpanna* corresponds to the Chinese *xiùtuóhuán*, which in the language of Tang means "the fruit of flowing against the current.

Because one flows against the stream of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), remains unstained by the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), and exclusively cultivates untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*), it is called the fruit of srotāpanna.
"If one realizes the dharma of signlessness, there is no mind that attains the fruit. Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this?
The *srotāpanna* is called 'one who has entered the stream,' yet there is nothing entered;
they do not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas. This is what is called being a *srotāpanna*. The Buddha again addressed Subhūti: "At..."
"What do you think? Can a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) give rise to such a thought of wisdom as, 'Have I attained the fruit of a *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner)'?
Subhūti understood the meaning. In the Sanskrit language, *srotāpanna* means "one who has entered the stream"; in the language of Tang, it is called the "fruit of once-returning.
Having abandoned the fetters of the three realms, one is named "one who goes once. One goes from the heavens back to the human world, and is born from the human world [back to the heavens].
Dying from the heavens is called the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin. If one realizes the dharma of signlessness, how could there be a mind that attains a fruit?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? A Sakṛdāgāmin is called 'one who comes and goes once,' yet in reality there is no coming or going;
it is merely designated as a Sakṛdāgāmin. The Buddha then addressed Subhūti again.
"What do you think? Can an *anāgāmin* give rise to such a thought of wisdom as, 'I have attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*'?
Subhūti, understand this: in Sanskrit, *anāgāmin* means in Chinese 'the fruit of non-returning' (*bùhuán guǒ*), and it is also called 'transcending desire' (*chūyù*).
To transcend desire means that externally one does not see objects of desire that can cause defilement, and internally there is no desiring mind that can be activated."
Because they will certainly not take rebirth in the desire realm, they are called "Non-returners" (Anāgāmin).
If one realizes the dharma of signlessness, how could there be a mind that attains a fruit? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because of the Anāgāmin..."
He is called "One Who Does Not Return" (*anāgāmin*). Yet, by their very nature, they are in reality not non-returning.
For this reason, he is named an *anāgāmin*. The Buddha addressed Subhūti again: "What do you think?
Is it possible for an arhat to have such a thought of wisdom as, 'I have attained the path of an arhat'? Subhūti understood the meaning of the Sanskrit term *arhat*.

In the language of Tang, this is called "Practice Without Strife" (araṇā-vihāra). It is also called "One Beyond Training" (aśaikṣa). With afflictions forever exhausted, one does not engage in strife with others;
greed, anger, and delusion are severed, and both mind and objects are empty. Being eternally tranquil internally and externally, such a person is named an Arhat.

If one harbors the thought of having attained this fruit, that is an Arhat who still possesses strife. Although such a person is beyond training, they remain attached to the realm of non-existence (asaṃskṛta-dhātu). Subhūti—
He replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because in reality there is not a single dharma that can be called 'Arhat.
World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to form such a thought of wisdom as, 'I have attained the path of Arhatship'..."
"World-Honored One, one would thereby be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span. World-Honored One, Subhūti said:
'The Buddha has declared that I am foremost among men in the attainment of the Samādhi of Non-Contention; I am a foremost Arhat free from desire.
World-Honored One, I do not harbor such a thought regarding prajñā as: 'I am an Arhat free from desire. What is this called?"
The Samādhi of Non-contention (araṇā-samādhi). This refers to an Arhat whose mind is without arising or ceasing, coming or going;

there is only the constant illumination of original enlightenment (mūla-avabodha), which constantly illuminates the emptiness and stillness of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha). This is called the Samādhi of Non-contention.
By cultivating this samādhi, one transcends the stage of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa) and becomes the foremost among men. If one harbors even a single thought of attaining the fruit, my fruit is lost.
