Dignified deportment is tranquil; the lamp of Prajñā wisdom is ignited. The fundamental source is pure and still; one remains eternally in silent samādhi.
O Buddha, within this realm nothing further arises. Before the tower of liberation, the mirror of Xuanyuan is hung up, universally illuminating the great earth and the cosmos.
Universally illuminating the great earth and the cosmos.
One whose deportment is tranquil must further kindle the lamp of wisdom to illuminate and shatter the afflictions of ignorance;
therefore, their deportment is tranquil. The Heart Sutra says: "Neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Therefore, within emptiness, it is said: "The fundamental source is originally pure. Furthermore, the practitioner must practice...
Whether standing, sitting, or reclining, he remains tranquil and unmoving. Once, while seated in meditative concentration, he realized the Buddha.
For such a person, objective realms no longer arise; this liberation is itself quiescence, and this quiescence is itself *prajñā*.
This *prajñā* is the original nature, which is empty space. The "mirror of Xuanyuan" is the Yellow Emperor of Xuanyuan.
The Emperor: "There is a single-sided mirror that reflects the liver-flower and the five viscera, their fatness or leanness, their squareness or roundness, and one's original nature.
It is likened to the mirror of Xuanyuan. One must use it to reflect and see through all afflictions, ignorance, affectionate attachments, and the seven emotions, thereby shattering them all.
Therefore it is said: 'Before the Tower of Liberation, hang up the mirror of Xuanyuan; the great earth and the cosmos are universally illuminated.'"
The principle of the unified totality (*ekaghanalakṣaṇa*) is like a person drinking water: its warmth is known by oneself; it is beyond comparison in the world.
The fundamental nature is a unified totality, forged into a single whole. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to grind the trichiliocosm into fine dust, what do you think? Would that be much dust?"
"Venerable One, would that mass of atoms not be considered many? Subhūti, grasping the Buddha’s intention, replied, "It would be very many, World-Honored One.
Why is this? If that mass of atoms were substantially real, the Buddha would not have called it a "mass of atoms. For what reason? This is a metaphor for the world [as] the Dharma-body.
The body. The metaphor of atoms refers to the form-body (*rūpakāya*); the world is one, while the atoms are many. By crushing the world into dust, the world ceases to exist;

yet when one regards the dust as the world, the dust lacks any distinct nature. For example, when the entirety of phenomena (*dharma*) arises as the response (*nirmāṇa*), the response lacks any distinct nature;
when the entirety of the response arises as phenomena, the phenomena lack any distinct nature. Unity and multiplicity are without difference. Thus the Buddha spoke of atoms.
"Multitudes of dust particles are not, in fact, multitudes of dust particles; they are the dust particles within the minds of sentient beings.
Just as there are dust particles in a trichiliocosm, these are said to be the deluded thoughts upon one's nature, and are not the dust particles of the physical world.
Within thought, that which is ever-present in purity is called 'dust particles. World-Honored One, as for the trichiliocosm spoken of by the Tathāgata..."
Regarding the "trichiliocosm" (great trichiliocosm): within the minds of sentient beings, there are one thousand instances each of greed, hatred, and delusion; this is not yet a world.
If greed, hatred, and delusion are exhausted, it is called a world. This refers to the greed, hatred, and delusion within the minds of these sentient beings.
It cannot be measured; therefore, it is called the "Great Trichiliocosm. Why is this?
If the world were truly existent, then the conjunction of the afflictions within the minds of these sentient beings would constitute a "unified whole" (*ekapiṇḍa*).

Yet, when the Tathāgata speaks of a unified whole, it is because the minds of sentient beings grasp at something; thus, it is not a unified whole. When the mind grasps at nothing, it is eternally pure. This is...
It is called a "unified mark. The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "That which is a unified mark is ineffable.
It is only ordinary people who greedily cling to unified marks; their arrogance, conceit, and disputes remain entirely unremoved.
To fixate on the recitation of words while failing to practice the Prajñāpāramitā—such a thing is impossible."
Therefore, regarding the principle of the unified totality (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*), worldly people do not understand this principle; it is difficult to explain and hard to believe. Thus it is said:
"When the Tathāgata drinks water, he knows its warmth or coolness by himself; there is no one in the world who can equal him."
The principle of the unified totality (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*) penetrates both nature and the Way;
A single jewel in the void illuminates the worlds of the ten directions throughout. The essence of all Buddhas of the three periods is one and the same.
For one who possesses this principle of the unified totality, both nature and the Way are thoroughly penetrated, and inner and outer are clearly transparent, fused into a single whole. There is no...
Above there is no below; there is no east, no west, no south, and no north—pure and luminous.
It is like a single precious jewel suspended in the midst of space, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.

Without "that" or "this," without high or low, from the immortals and Buddhas above down to the insects below, all are unified within this single Dharma-body; therefore, it is called the Three Periods of Time.

The essence of all Buddhas is one and the same; it is the principle of the unified totality (*ekasaṃnipāta*). In the past, King Liang failed to recognize the occasion [of the teaching] and the intent of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West. He crossed the river by breaking a reed and went away;
the Buddha sat facing a wall for more than nine years. From patriarch to patriarch it was transmitted, their lamps and lights constantly meeting. A single flower blooms.
Five petals aligned. When a single flower blooms, the five petals are aligned.
The original nature is unified and forged into a single whole. There is no further cultivation or realization. The Buddha said, "Subhūti, that which is a unified whole is ineffable;
it is only ordinary people who are greedily attached to such things. [This refers to] the self and others.

Arrogance, greedy attachment, and seeking after things; regarding phenomena as a unified whole, one then says, "I can" and "I understand," "I have awakened" and "I have attained," and engages in notions of self, others, right, and wrong.
For this reason, it cannot be spoken of. Formerly, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty summoned Bodhidharma.
The Emperor asked, "I have built monasteries, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks beyond counting. What merit do these bring? The Master replied:
"It possesses no merit. The Emperor asked, "How can it be without merit? The Master replied, "This is merely a minor fruit of the human or celestial realms, a cause of out-flowing (sāsrava) karma.
It follows one like a shadow follows a form; though it exists, it is not real. The Emperor asked, "What, then, is true merit?"
The Master said, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and tranquil. Such merit is not to be sought through worldly means.
The Emperor further asked, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? The Master replied, "Vast and open—there is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that faces me?
The Master said, "I do not know. The Emperor did not understand. The Master, knowing their faculties were not in accord, broke a reed and passed it across [the water].
Bodhidharma dwelt at Shaolin Temple, sitting facing a wall for more than nine years. Thereafter, he transmitted [the Dharma] to the Second Patriarch, Huike;
the Third Patriarch, Sengcan; the Fourth Patriarch, Daoxin; the Fifth Patriarch, Hongren; and the Sixth Patriarch, Huineng, continuing down to the present day.
Thus it is said: "A single flower blooms, and the five petals unfold together."
When knowledge and views do not arise, one borrows the provisional to cultivate the real; this profound and subtle transmission transforms iron into gold.
When everything is forged into a single piece right here and now, knowledge and views naturally cease to arise. The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If someone were to say that the Buddha has taught the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span—Subhūti, [regard them as speaking falsely]."

"What do you think? Does this person understand the meaning of what I have said? Subhūti, grasping the Buddha’s intention—that the Tathāgata possesses a true fourfold view that differs from that of ordinary people—replied, "No, World-Honored One. This person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has said.
Why is this? Because the World-Honored One speaks of the true view of self, the view of a person, and the view of a sentient being."

The view of a self that lasts for a lifetime (*jīvadr̥ṣṭi*) is not the deluded self. "Self" refers to the view of a person (*pudgaladṛṣṭi*), the view of a sentient being (*sattvadṛṣṭi*), and the view of a self that lasts for a lifetime (*jīvadr̥ṣṭi*).

If one is such a person, they clearly understand that from the ultimate truth (*tattva*) arises delusion, and from delusion arises the ultimate truth; yet truth and delusion are not distinguished, merging into one.
This is what the Tathāgata calls the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span.
He speaks thus so that all sentient beings may awaken for themselves and cultivate the true wisdom of prajñā; therefore, he says there are four true views.
When the Tathāgata says that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, this is the true view of self. When he says that all sentient beings possess the untainted [dharmas],...
"Wisdom-nature" is the view of a true person. To say that all sentient beings fundamentally possess no afflictions is the view of a true sentient being.
To say that the original nature of all sentient beings is indestructible throughout ten thousand kalpas is the view of a true life-span possessor (*jīvaka*).
Ordinary people do not understand the Buddha’s intention. The Buddha again addressed Subhūti, [instructing him] to aspire to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding the third, the bodhicitta: with respect to all Buddha-dharmas, one should not be attached to either the real or the false. Knowing thus, one is unattached to the real or the false;
seeing thus, one is unattached to the real or the false; resolving with faith thus, although one liberates sentient beings, one does not give rise to the mark of preaching the Dharma.
Subhūti, as for what is called the "mark of preaching the Dharma," it is the mind of subject and object returning [to its source].
To preach the Dharma while not apprehending the characteristics of the Dharma—that is, when neither the subjective mind nor the objective mind arises—is what is called preaching the Dharma.

Therefore, seeing and knowing do not arise. As for "borrowing the provisional to cultivate the real," this refers to the profound and wondrous principle taught by the Tathāgata, which leads people to realize their nature without departing from the physical body.
If one does not understand the physical body, where could one cultivate the Way? Hence it is said: "Borrow the provisional to cultivate the real."

The physical body of an ordinary person is like a block of raw iron. Due to ignorance and afflictions, arrogance and conceit, the sense of self and notions of right and wrong, and greed, anger, and delusive thoughts, there is the cycle of rebirth in the hells. This is the profound and subtle principle of the Tathāgata.
It illuminates and shatters ignorance and afflictions, pride and arrogance, and the distinctions between self and others; thus one attains Buddhahood.
Therefore, this profound and wondrous transmission transforms iron into gold.
When the power of non-arising knowledge-and-vision is abundant, one leaves the sea of suffering and departs from the Sahā world;
with a single great roar, one strikes like a thunderclap. The Ten Courts of King Yama are helpless before such a person whose knowledge-and-vision does not arise.
Such a person shares the same cultivation and realization as the Buddhas of the three periods of time, truly realizing Bodhi.
Therefore it is said: "The power of the non-arising of knowledge and vision is great. Such a person leaves behind the sea of suffering and exits the Sahā world.
If one lets out a great roar, like the crash of thunder and lightning, one gathers empty space back into oneself;
the entire body becomes a single state of pure voidness. Therefore it is said: "The Ten Halls of King Yama have no recourse against him; he must be seized and brought up."
Without attachment, knowledge and vision do not arise. Having recited this single scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra*, everyone pays equal respect; each person listens with a steadfast mind.
The seeds of Buddhahood reside within the eight merits. The five aggregates are all empty; when the ground of the mind is as clear as a mirror, who fears King Yama?

Discussing worldly sentiments—even if one were to discuss worldly sentiments before King Yama—to have no arising of conceptual views is precisely to cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā Dharma. This is the single fascicle of the *Vajra*.
Speaking solely of the Prajñāpāramitā Dharma, it is condensed into four-line verses;

for this reason, I have chanted this single scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra* and earnestly exhorted the great assembly not to let this precious time pass in vain. Thus it is said: "May everyone pay equal respect;
may each person listen with a steadfast mind. My Buddha-seed is planted within the eight fields of merit, to serve as the foundation for Bodhi."
The seeds. As for the eight fields of merit: great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity—these four immeasurable minds—plus the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths;
when these are all devoid of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, they are called the eight fields of merit.

This is the field of the mind. Regarding the emptiness of the five aggregates: this refers to the absence of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. If one attains illumination...
Seeing that the five aggregates are empty, one transcends the realm of birth and death, escapes the suffering of saṃsāra, and accomplishes the unsurpassed path.
For one whose mind-ground is as clear as a mirror, the practitioner’s mirror of mind reflects through and shatters afflictions and ignorance.
Self-grasping, deluded arrogance, fondness for valor, and the distinctions of "I" and "you"—if one acts in such ways, what fear need one have of King Yama?
To discuss worldly sentiments is but a provisional manifestation and not the truth. To see one's nature and clarify the mind is to transcend the three realms; this is the pure Dharma-body.
The response-body and transformation-bodies are likewise not ultimate reality. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"If there were someone who took the seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and offered them as a gift, this would result in the meritorious rewards of gods and humans;
such merit, though great, is subject to exhaustion. However, if there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon the bodhicitta and maintains this..."

The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, even just these four lines of verse and so forth—should one receive and uphold them, read and recite them with mindfulness, and explain them for others, benefiting all sentient beings, their merit will surpass that [of the former].
It would surpass the merit of giving the seven treasures to people throughout incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds. How does one explain them for others? Simply...
This is the teaching for people: not to grasp at any marks. The self-nature is suchness (*tathatā*), immovable.

This mind of suchness, immovable, is without a mind of seeking, without a mind of arising and ceasing, and without a mind of joy or anger. Because the one mind is immovable, it is called "suchness, immovable. Why is this?
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew.
It is also like lightning; one should contemplate it in this way. The dream is the deluded body; the illusion is deluded thought; the bubble is affliction;
the shadow is like karmic obstruction; the dew and lightning are that which vanishes in an instant.

These—dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, dew, and lightning—are called conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). How could they be permanent? Reality is free from names and marks; this is what the awakened one realizes.

This is indeed the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). It is titled the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life. Therefore, the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and transformation-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) are not the true [body].
If one is a practitioner who does not grasp at any marks (*nimitta*), their own mind will be suchness (*tathatā*) and unmoving; they will certainly perceive their nature and clarify their mind.
If one attains the vision of one's nature and the illumination of the mind, one achieves the Buddha-way.
Practicing in this manner, one transcends the triple world and reveals the pure Dharma-body. *Tut!* If you wish to transcend the triple world, let there not be even a single point of mind.
When you practice in this way, all affairs will be brought to completion.
The response-body and transformation-body are not the true; one must realize the three bodies. Ten thousand paths of radiant light shine as a single expanse of clarity;
the myriad phenomena of the universe appear before one’s eyes, manifesting the sixteen-foot purple-gold body.
These response and transformation bodies are not the reality; they are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, dew, and lightning—how could they be considered permanent?
Furthermore, this pure *dharmakāya* is also a provisional name; thus it is said: "The response-body and transformation-body are not the true [body]; one realizes the three bodies as one.
If the internal and external are interconnected and forged into a single whole, it is like ten thousand rays of rosy light forming a single expanse of brilliance.
Look, look! The stars, planets, sun, moon, wind, and rain; heaven and earth, the world; spring brings forth life.
In summer there is growth, in autumn there is harvest, and in winter there is storage. Therefore, the myriad phenomena of the universe manifest directly before one.
*Tut!* What is it that manifests? *Ei!* It is none other than the sixteen-foot purple-gold body of Śākyamuni Buddha.

Emanations are not the ultimate reality. May all people universally repay the four debts of gratitude. May the winds be harmonious and the rains timely. Parents bestow the physical body and provide instruction;
the Buddha bestows the light that illuminates like the sun and moon. May the Buddha-Dharma flourish and firmly stabilize heaven and earth.
We offer our prayers for the Emperor’s reign to endure ten thousand myriad springs. We offer our prayers.
"Resplendent ten thousand myriad springs.
To hold that transformation is not real is to immediately realize that conditions are illusory; hence it is said: "The manifested transformation is not real.

As for the "responding body" (nirmāṇakāya), this refers to the physical body composed of the four great elements. The "transformed body" (nirmāṇakāya) exists within this physical body, performing such functions as welcoming guests and entertaining visitors through deliberation and thought.
This is a calculated [expedient]. Although it is an *nirmāṇakāya* (manifestation), it is not the true body;

from where else could it come? Therefore, it is said: "May all people universally repay the four debts of gratitude. As for these four debts of gratitude: the debt of the Heaven and Earth for providing shelter and support; the debt of the Sun and Moon for their illumination; the debt of the King for the land and water;
and the debt of one's parents for giving birth to this body. Furthermore, may they protect and sustain us so that the winds and rains are harmonious and the state is at peace.
May the realm be peaceful and the people at ease. Furthermore, I exhort the great assembly to be filial and obedient toward their parents;
may my Buddha protect and cause the Dharma to flourish, so as to stabilize heaven and earth. I further offer prayers for the Emperor’s reign to endure ten thousand myriad springs.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all the world— including devas, humans, and asuras— having heard what the Buddha taught,
were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
